_readme: Queue for the daily blog routine. It takes the first entry with status 'queued',
writes the post as content/blog/<slug>.json, runs the duplicate gate, and on a
pass marks it 'published'. On a gate failure it marks it 'rejected' with the
score and moves to the next topic — a rejected topic is one that turned out to
be a restatement of something already on the site.
HONEST CEILING — read before adding filler.
These topics are things a Melbourne painter of 18 years actually knows and a
homeowner actually searches. That supply is finite. There are perhaps 60-80
genuinely distinct, genuinely useful articles about residential painting in one
city. At 30 posts a month this queue is exhausted in roughly ten to twelve
weeks. After that the choices are: slow down, expand scope (commercial, strata,
trade-facing), or start publishing recombinations that the duplicate gate will
reject anyway. Do not pad the queue to hit a number - an empty queue is a
signal, not a bug, and the routine reports it rather than inventing topics.
Each topic carries an 'angle' because the topic alone is not enough to keep
posts distinct. The angle is the specific claim the article makes.

topics.title: Spray or Brush? When Each Belongs
topics.angle: Jetblack's actual working rule: spray when the property is empty and maskable, brush and roll when people are living in it. The trade-off is finish quality against disruption, not one method being better.

topics.title: Can You Paint Through a Melbourne Winter?
topics.angle: Yes, with constraints. Surface temperature and dew point matter more than air temperature; the real limits are drying windows and overnight condensation, not the calendar.

topics.title: Matt, Low Sheen, Satin, Gloss: Which Goes Where
topics.angle: Sheen is a durability and light decision, not a taste one. Where each belongs room by room, and why 'flat' is a sheen level rather than a description of a smooth finish.

topics.title: Why Exterior Paint Fails: Reading the Symptoms
topics.angle: Blistering, flaking, chalking and cracking each have a different cause and a different fix. Diagnosing which one you have before repainting is what stops it recurring.

topics.title: Painting Over Dark Walls Without Six Coats
topics.angle: Coverage is a primer problem, not a paint-quality problem. Tinted undercoat does in one coat what three topcoats will not.

topics.title: Why Timber Window Frames Fail First
topics.angle: Sills and lower rails take standing water and the most UV, so they fail years before the wall does. Spot repair versus full strip, and when each is right.

topics.title: Painting With Kids and Pets in the House
topics.angle: Low-VOC and low-odour paints have closed most of the gap on durability. What actually reduces disruption is sequencing rooms and ventilation, not the product alone.

topics.title: Repainting a Rental Between Tenants
topics.angle: The brief is different from an owner-occupier repaint: turnaround and durability beat colour ambition, and a washable low sheen outlives a fashionable matt.

topics.title: Cracks That Keep Coming Back
topics.angle: Cornice and join cracks are movement, not paint failure. Filler alone will always reopen; the fix depends on whether the movement is seasonal or structural.

topics.title: Painting Rendered Walls Without Trapping Moisture
topics.angle: Render needs to breathe. Sealing it with the wrong membrane traps moisture behind the coating and causes the blistering people blame on the paint.

topics.title: Why Every White Looks Different in Your House
topics.angle: Whites carry undertones that shift with orientation and light. North and south facing rooms need different whites to read as the same colour.

topics.title: Lead Paint in Pre-1970 Melbourne Homes
topics.angle: Sanding old paint without testing is the actual risk. How to identify likely lead layers and what changes about preparation when they are present.

topics.title: Painting a Home Under a Heritage Overlay
topics.angle: An overlay constrains colour and sometimes method. Check before quoting, because repainting a non-compliant scheme twice is the expensive outcome.

topics.title: Dry to Touch Is Not Cured
topics.angle: Paint is touch-dry in hours and fully cured in weeks. Washing, taping or reinstalling hardware too early is a common way to ruin a good job.

topics.title: Painting a Bathroom That Stays Painted
topics.angle: Ventilation decides the outcome more than the paint does. What to fix before painting, and why anti-mould primer is not optional on a bathroom ceiling.

topics.title: Painting Brick: Know That It Is Permanent
topics.angle: Paint on brick is effectively irreversible - stripping is costly and rarely complete. Worth doing deliberately, not as a quick cosmetic fix.

topics.title: How a Body Corporate Repaint Actually Runs
topics.angle: The painting is the easy part. Scope agreement, access to occupied units and staged scheduling are what determine whether it finishes on time.

topics.title: Painting a Trading Business Without Closing It
topics.angle: After-hours and staged work costs more per hour and less overall, because the alternative is lost trading days.

topics.title: Repainting a Front Door Properly
topics.angle: A door is a small job with unusually visible failure. Removing hardware, working horizontally where possible, and respecting cure time before closing it.

topics.title: Matching a Colour You No Longer Have
topics.angle: Scanning a chip gets close but ages and fades mislead the reader. Where to take the sample from, and why a patch test still matters.

topics.title: Eaves and Fascia: The Part Everyone Skips
topics.angle: Eaves are shaded, rarely washed by rain, and collect mould and dust. Skipping them is why a freshly painted house still looks tired.

topics.title: How Many Coats Do You Actually Need?
topics.angle: Two topcoats over a correct primer is the honest answer for most surfaces. Where a third genuinely earns its place, and where it is padding.

topics.title: Fence: Paint It or Stain It?
topics.angle: Stain fails gracefully and recoats easily; paint looks sharper and fails badly. The right choice depends on how often you will maintain it.

topics.title: Nail Pops and Visible Joins
topics.angle: New-build settlement pushes fixings through the surface in the first years. Fixing the fixing, not just the dent, is what stops it returning.

topics.title: What Access Does to an Exterior Quote
topics.angle: Height, pitch and clearance drive scaffolding, and scaffolding drives cost more than paint does. Why two similar-looking houses quote very differently.

topics.title: Stains That Bleed Back Through Fresh Paint
topics.angle: Rust, tannin from cedar and water stains all reappear through water-based topcoats. A stain-blocking primer is the only reliable answer.

topics.title: What Makes a Cabinet Finish Look Factory-Made
topics.angle: The glass-smooth look on cabinetry comes from spray application and dust control, not from a premium tin. Why brushed cabinet doors always read as brushed.

topics.title: Painting Before You Sell: Where the Return Is
topics.angle: Buyers price visible condition. Entry, main living and street-facing exterior carry the return; repainting every bedroom rarely does.

topics.title: How Often Weatherboards Really Need Repainting
topics.angle: Orientation decides the cycle. The north and west elevations fail years before the south, and spot-recoating them beats waiting for the whole house.

topics.title: Reading a Painting Quote Line by Line
topics.angle: Scope, not price, is where quotes differ. What each line should specify, and which omissions predict a dispute.
